summary: This RFC describes how Internet mail systems route messages using information from the domain system, in particular how mailers interpret MX records. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 2821.

plainLanguage.summary: Before the domain system, mail servers could assume that mail addressed to a machine went to that machine. This RFC explains the arrangement that replaced it: the DNS holds MX records that list, for a domain name, the hosts that accept its mail and a number saying in which order to try them.

questions: how do mx records route mail
how does mail routing work with dns
how does a mailer choose which mx to try
subtitle: How a mail server was told to pick the right host to deliver a message to.

tldr.problem: Under the earlier mail system, a mailer could assume that a message addressed to a host could be delivered by connecting to that host. That failed for hosts not directly attached to the Internet, and the domain system had no agreed way of saying where mail should really go.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains how to read MX resource records, which match a domain name with a preference value and a host name. A mailer queries for the records, drops any that would loop the mail back to itself, and tries the rest in order of preference.
tldr.outcome: RFC 974 is a Historic document from January 1986 and has been obsoleted by RFC 2821, which restates the requirements for Internet mail routing.

facts.label: Delivery order
facts.value: The lowest preference value is tried first

facts.label: Empty MX list
facts.value: Treated as one MX with preference 0 for the destination itself

facts.label: Loop prevention
facts.value: Deliver only to an MX with a lower preference than your own

facts.label: Ties
facts.value: All MXs at one preference are tried before any higher one

facts.label: Other record types used
facts.value: CNAME for aliases and WKS for supported services

today: RFC 974 is a Historic document from January 1986, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 2821, which restates the requirements for Internet mail routing. The memo itself is a set of guidelines rather than a protocol specification, and it leaves the behaviour for each kind of query error to the implementor.

sections.title: Why Mail Routing Needed the Domain System
sections.content:
This memo explains how mail systems on the Internet were expected to route messages using information from the domain system, and in particular how a mailer should read MX resource records. It says nothing about how to interpret MB and MG records, which were used for mailbox names.

The need arose from a change in the assumptions behind mail addresses. Under RFC 882 and RFC 883, a mailer could usually assume that a message addressed to a mailbox could be delivered by opening an SMTP connection to that host. That broke down for hosts not directly attached to the Internet, such as certain UUCP and CSNET hosts, which could only be handled as special cases in configuration files.

With the domain system in place, a mailer cannot simply connect to the named host. It has to ask the domain system where messages for that name should be delivered, and the answer may name a completely different host, or offer a choice of routes. The memo is a set of guidelines for how a mailer should behave in that more complicated world, and it assumes the reader knows RFCs 882 and 883 and the updates to them.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail used to be simple: the name in the address was the machine to connect to. The domain system made that unreliable, so a separate record had to say where mail for a name should really go.

sections.title: What the Domain Servers Store
sections.content:
The domain servers store information as a series of resource records, each holding one piece of information about a given domain name, which is usually but not always a host. The simplest way to think of a record is a typed pair: a domain name matched with relevant data, stored with type information so that systems can tell when it is relevant.

For message routing the system stores MX records. Each MX matches a domain name with two pieces of data: a preference value, an unsigned 16-bit integer, and the name of a host. The preference number indicates the order in which a mailer should try the hosts, with the lowest numbered MX tried first. Several MX records may share the same preference value and then have the same priority.

Two other record types may be encountered. The canonical name record states that the queried name is an alias for another name, the proper one. The Well Known Service record holds information about the network services a given domain name supports, such as SMTP.
sections.plainLanguage: The record for a domain name holds a number and a host name. The number is the order: the smallest number is tried first, and several hosts may share the same number and so the same priority.

sections.title: Issuing the Query and Reading the Answer
sections.content:
The explanation is framed around a mailer on a host named LOCAL trying to deliver a message to a domain named REMOTE, where LOCAL is the mailer's own official name and not an alias.

The first step is to query for the MX records of REMOTE, and the memo strongly urges that this be done every time a delivery is attempted, so that changes to the domain database take effect quickly and an administrator can re-route messages in transit to a defective host simply by changing the database.

Three responses count as errors. Getting no response at all is an error, which is different from an answer that simply contains no answers to the query. A response with the truncation bit set is an error, because the answer section may be missing critical records; such a response may not be used and the query should be repeated over a virtual circuit instead of a datagram. A response with a non-zero response code is an error.

The memo does not fix the behaviour for each error, but suggests that they be treated differently: a response code of non-existent domain should probably return the message to the sender as invalid, while a server failure should probably cause a retry later. One special case is not an error: if the answer contains a canonical name record, then REMOTE is an alias for another name and the query should be repeated with the canonical name.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask for the records every time, so that a change of address takes effect at once. Three things count as a failed lookup: no answer at all, an answer that was cut short, and an answer that reports an error.

sections.title: Choosing Which Host to Deliver To
sections.content:
If the answer contains no MX records at all, the mailer treats the list as if it held a single record with preference 0 and a host name of REMOTE, and attempts delivery there without further processing. The idea is that a domain which advertises nothing about a name is given the benefit of the doubt.

If the list is not empty, irrelevant records are removed in two steps, and the order matters. First, a Well Known Service query may be issued for each MX to see whether that host really supports the mail service wanted; records naming hosts that do not are discarded. This step is optional but strongly encouraged. Second, if the mailer's own host LOCAL appears as an MX, every MX with a preference value greater than or equal to LOCAL's own is discarded.

That second rule is the main defence against mail looping. A mailer on a host that is itself listed as an MX may only deliver to an MX with a lower preference count than its own. If the list is now empty, that is an error: either the service queries found that no listed host supports mail, or the domain system believes LOCAL is handling mail for REMOTE while the mailer on LOCAL is not set up for it. How a mailer handles this is left to the implementor.

If records remain, the mailer tries them in order of preference and is required to attempt the lowest valued one. Implementors are encouraged to try them all until one accepts the message or all have been tried. Where several MXs share a preference value, all of them must be tried before any higher value is tried, and all of the lowest ones must be tried before the message is deemed undeliverable.
sections.plainLanguage: Two clean-up steps come before delivery. Hosts that do not accept mail are dropped, and any host whose number is not lower than the sending host's own number is dropped, which is what stops mail bouncing between two servers. What is left is tried in order, and ties are all tried before moving on.

sections.title: Three Worked Examples
sections.content:
The memo works through three cases against one database. A.EXAMPLE.ORG has MX records for itself with preference 10, for B.EXAMPLE.ORG with preference 15 and for C.EXAMPLE.ORG with preference 20. B.EXAMPLE.ORG has MX records for itself with preference 0 and for C.EXAMPLE.ORG with preference 10. C.EXAMPLE.ORG has an MX for itself with preference 0. D.EXAMPLE.ORG has two MX records, both with preference 0, one for itself and one for C.EXAMPLE.ORG.

In the first case a mailer on D.EXAMPLE.ORG is sending to A.EXAMPLE.ORG. D.EXAMPLE.ORG is not among the MX records and all three support SMTP, so none is eliminated. The mailer must try A.EXAMPLE.ORG first because it has the lowest value, and may then try B.EXAMPLE.ORG and C.EXAMPLE.ORG.

In the second case the mailer is on B.EXAMPLE.ORG sending to A.EXAMPLE.ORG. In A.EXAMPLE.ORG's list B.EXAMPLE.ORG appears with preference 15 and C.EXAMPLE.ORG with preference 20, so both are at or above B's own value of 15 and both records are discarded. Only A.EXAMPLE.ORG, with preference 10, is left, and that is the only host it can try.

In the third case a mailer on A.EXAMPLE.ORG is sending to D.EXAMPLE.ORG. There are two MX records and both have the same preference value, so either will accept mail. The mailer tries one, and if that fails tries the other.
sections.plainLanguage: The three examples cover the interesting cases: a sender that is not among the destinations, a sender that is, and a destination with two hosts tied on the same number. Each comes out with a different list of hosts to try.

messages.note: The memo strongly urges a fresh query for every delivery attempt.

messages.label: Answer: a list of MX records
Drop entries not lower than its own preference
messages.note: This is the rule that prevents mail from looping.

messages.label: Deliver to the lowest preference host
Try the next one if that fails
messages.note: All hosts sharing the lowest preference are tried before any with a higher one.

viz.caption: WHAT COUNTS AS AN ERROR WHEN QUERYING (RFC 974)

items.label: No answer at all
items.desc: The domain server never sends anything back. This is different from an answer that contains no answers to the query.

items.label: Truncated answer
items.desc: The truncation bit in the header is set, so critical records may be missing. The response may not be used and the query should be repeated over a virtual circuit.

items.label: Error response
items.desc: A non-existent domain should probably return the message to the sender as invalid; a server failure should probably cause a retry later.

items.label: Alias
items.desc: The answer contains a canonical name record, so the destination is an alias and the query should be repeated with the canonical name.

items.label: No MX records
items.desc: Treat it as a single MX with preference 0 for the destination itself, and attempt delivery there.

cells: A.EXAMPLE.ORG first, then B.EXAMPLE.ORG and C.EXAMPLE.ORG
One of the two, then the other
